 4,188.30 +0.04%   10/1/2026, 6:27:16 AM ET       Treasury trouble   Who among us hasn’t had an awkward day at their new job? Spare a thought, then, for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.

   He annoyed the man who hired him, President Trump, by voting along with colleagues to hike rates in September. Traders were betting they’d do it again this month, but now mostly aren’t. What changed?

   An obvious reason is that someone nearly as influential as Warsh just told us so . John Williams, vice chair of the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee, said Tuesday he sees “no need for urgency.” October rate-hike odds fell to just 38%, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, barely half what they’d been a week earlier.

   His remarks came as a surprise because the two data releases most likely to influence the Fed’s decision were still pending—Wednesday’s PCE inflation number and Friday’s jobs report. PCE was basically in line. Economists think nonfarm payrolls grew by about 80,000 last month—no blowout, but enough to keep unemployment steady.

   Dig deeper, though, and you can see why the Fed might have held fire anyway. First, there’s the effect of recently surging Treasury yields on the economy. The 10-year note and 30-year bond both just hit levels not seen since 2002.

   That affects everything from housing, already in a funk, to the AI build-out, currently in whatever the opposite of a funk is. It’s now “the biggest bet in U.S. economic history,” as a recent must-read Journal article describes it.

   Data center construction is great for people and companies paid to build, equip and power them. AI itself is expected to have real economic benefits, too, but its biggest effect right now is trillions in paper stock-market wealth boosting spending by well-off Americans. 

   A recent report by the JPMorganChase Institute shows that the share of people making withdrawals from investment accounts to checking accounts nearly doubled this April compared with the same month in 2019. That hinges on stock prices staying high. The wealth effect only indirectly helps people who rely on wage income.

   Today’s “no fire, slow hire” job market looks strong, but it doesn’t feel that way. The Conference Board’s survey of consumer confidence in September showed the biggest differential between answers to the question “jobs are plentiful” and “jobs are hard to get” in more than five years.

   Purely on the most-watched numbers, unemployment at 4.1% and PCE inflation a full percentage point above its target, the Fed’s textbook move now is still to hike. But Warsh has cover to play it safe at the next meeting, which comes at a politically touchy time anyway—six days before midterm elections.

   If signs of economic weakness are more obvious by the December meeting then he might be off the hook for standing pat. The rest of us might not feel as relieved.

Treasury trouble

 

Who among us hasn’t had an awkward day at their new job? Spare a thought, then, for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.

 

He annoyed the man who hired him, President Trump, by voting along with colleagues to hike rates in September. Traders were betting they’d do it again this month, but now mostly aren’t. What changed?

 

An obvious reason is that someone nearly as influential as Warsh just told us so. John Williams, vice chair of the Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee, said Tuesday he sees “no need for urgency.” October rate-hike odds fell to just 38%, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, barely half what they’d been a week earlier.

 

His remarks came as a surprise because the two data releases most likely to influence the Fed’s decision were still pending—Wednesday’s PCE inflation number and Friday’s jobs report. PCE was basically in line. Economists think nonfarm payrolls grew by about 80,000 last month—no blowout, but enough to keep unemployment steady.

 

Dig deeper, though, and you can see why the Fed might have held fire anyway. First, there’s the effect of recently surging Treasury yields on the economy. The 10-year note and 30-year bond both just hit levels not seen since 2002.

 

That affects everything from housing, already in a funk, to the AI build-out, currently in whatever the opposite of a funk is. It’s now “the biggest bet in U.S. economic history,” as a recent must-read Journal article describes it.

 

Data center construction is great for people and companies paid to build, equip and power them. AI itself is expected to have real economic benefits, too, but its biggest effect right now is trillions in paper stock-market wealth boosting spending by well-off Americans. 

 

A recent report by the JPMorganChase Institute shows that the share of people making withdrawals from investment accounts to checking accounts nearly doubled this April compared with the same month in 2019. That hinges on stock prices staying high. The wealth effect only indirectly helps people who rely on wage income.

 

Today’s “no fire, slow hire” job market looks strong, but it doesn’t feel that way. The Conference Board’s survey of consumer confidence in September showed the biggest differential between answers to the question “jobs are plentiful” and “jobs are hard to get” in more than five years.

 

Purely on the most-watched numbers, unemployment at 4.1% and PCE inflation a full percentage point above its target, the Fed’s textbook move now is still to hike. But Warsh has cover to play it safe at the next meeting, which comes at a politically touchy time anyway—six days before midterm elections.

 

If signs of economic weakness are more obvious by the December meeting then he might be off the hook for standing pat. The rest of us might not feel as relieved.
